rationale: A wins because it finds the uncomfortable story a real reporter may actually prefer: "What 40 chain optometry clinics mean for the independent eye doctor down the street." B is clean and useful, but its strongest healthcare frame, "Warby Parker's next act is eye exams, not frames," stays closer to Warby's own preferred narrative. A gives the founder sharper proof demands and better downside warnings; B gives tidy beat buckets.
gaps_in_A: "What 40 chain optometry clinics mean" overstates the supplied fact. The update says most of the 40 new stores will offer exams, not all 40.
"declining to break out exam revenue" assigns motive. The fact is only that exam-revenue contribution is not broken out.
"Warby was the canonical case study" and "proved you don't need stores" rely on outside brand history, not the supplied update.
"retail chains are absorbing routine eye care" is a strong thesis, but it needs external market evidence before it becomes more than a Warby-shaped hunch.
gaps_in_B: "Warby Parker's founding pitch was eliminating the middleman" is plausible lore, but it is not in the update. Ground it or soften it.
"the death of a retail thesis" overplays the evidence. The facts challenge the DTC thesis; they do not bury it with a shovel.
It misses the independent-optometry antagonist angle. That is the conflict story most likely to pull in outside voices and make the piece reportable.
"pharmacy chains' fight to reinvent the front of store" imports a current-retail peg without sourcing. Good instinct, but unsupported as written.
